steps.title: Create a TypeScript file and define a basic object literal
steps.instruction: Create a new TypeScript file and define a simple object literal named 'colors' with color names as keys and their hex values as strings.
steps.hint: Start with 'const colors = {' then add key-value pairs like 'red: "#ff0000",' inside curly braces.
steps.seedCode: // Define your colors object literal here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a 'colors' object with color names and hex values, ready for type-safe enhancement in later steps.
successCriteria: The 'colors' object is defined with at least two color-hex pairs (e.g., red and blue).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a basic object literal. This is the foundation we'll make type-safe with 'as const'.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure 'colors' is an object with color names as keys and hex strings as values.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create an object named 'colors' with properties like 'red: "#ff0000"' inside curly braces.

steps.title: Add type annotations to the object literal
steps.instruction: Add a type annotation to the colors object using a type alias or interface. Define a type alias or interface first, then apply it to the colors object.
steps.hint: Create a type alias with 'type ColorObject = { ... }' or an interface with 'interface ColorObject { ... }', then add ': ColorObject' after the colors object declaration.
steps.seedCode:
// Define your colors object literal here

// Add a type annotation to the colors object
steps.expectedOutcome: The colors object will have explicit type annotations using a type alias or interface.
successCriteria: A type alias or interface is defined and applied to the colors object with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added type annotations to the colors object, making its structure explicit.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to both define a type alias/interface AND apply it to the colors object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The type annotation is missing or incorrect. Remember to define a type alias or interface and apply it to the colors object.

steps.title: Demonstrate the limitation of mutable object literals
steps.instruction: Add a line of code that reassigns one of the color values in your object to demonstrate mutability.
steps.hint: After your object definition, write something like colors.primary = 'newColor' to show the value can be changed.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will show that object literal values can be mutated after creation, which can lead to unexpected behavior.
successCriteria: One of the color values is reassigned with a new string value using dot notation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've demonstrated how object literals can be mutated, which is a limitation we'll address with const assertions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're reassigning one of the existing properties (like colors.primary) to a new string value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try reassigning one of the color values. For example: colors.primary = 'red' would change the primary color value.

steps.title: Introduce the 'as const' assertion
steps.instruction: Add the 'as const' assertion to the colors object to make it deeply readonly.
steps.hint: Append 'as const' after the closing brace of the colors object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The colors object will now be treated as a deeply readonly literal type, preventing any reassignment of its properties.
successCriteria: The colors object has 'as const' appended to it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The 'as const' assertion makes the object deeply readonly, turning its properties into literal types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure 'as const' is placed directly after the object's closing brace.
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'as const' assertion is missing. Add it after the object to enforce immutability.

steps.title: Examine the resulting type with 'as const'
steps.instruction: Add a console.log statement to inspect the type of the colors object after the 'as const' assertion.
steps.hint: Use console.log with typeof to log the type of the colors object.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will see that the type of colors is now a read-only object with literal string types for its properties.
successCriteria: A console.log statement is added that logs the type of the colors object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully inspected the type. Notice how 'as const' makes the types 'blue' and 'green' instead of just string.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added console.log, but make sure you're logging the type of the colors object, not just the object itself.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding a console.log to inspect the type. Try using typeof colors in your console.log.

steps.title: Create a function that uses the const-asserted object
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'getColorHex' that takes a color key from the 'colors' object as a parameter and returns the corresponding hex value. Use the 'colors' object inside the function to demonstrate type safety.
steps.hint: Define a function with a parameter typed as a key of the 'colors' object, then return the value from the 'colors' object using that key.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that accepts a valid color key and returns the corresponding value, with TypeScript ensuring type safety.
successCriteria: A function named 'getColorHex' is defined, takes a parameter typed as a key of 'colors', and returns the value from 'colors' using that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a type-safe function that uses the const-asserted object. TypeScript now ensures only valid color keys can be passed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but check that it properly uses the 'colors' object and has the correct parameter type. Make sure the parameter is typed as a key of 'colors'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Ensure you create a function named 'getColorHex' that takes a color key parameter and returns the corresponding value from the 'colors' object.

steps.title: Compare with TypeScript enums
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript enum named 'ColorsEnum' that has the same values as your 'colors' object (primary: 'blue', secondary: 'green').
steps.hint: Use the 'enum' keyword followed by the enum name and curly braces containing the key-value pairs.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a TypeScript enum that mirrors the structure of your 'as const' object, allowing you to compare their syntax and behavior.
successCriteria: A TypeScript enum named 'ColorsEnum' is defined with 'primary' and 'secondary' members having string values 'blue' and 'green'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a TypeScript enum that matches your 'as const' object structure. This sets up the comparison we'll explore next.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your enum has both 'primary' and 'secondary' members with the correct string values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The enum definition doesn't match the expected structure. Remember to use the 'enum' keyword and include both color values.

steps.title: Create a union type from the const-asserted object
steps.instruction: Create a union type named 'ColorKey' that extracts all the keys from the 'colors' object using 'keyof typeof' syntax.
steps.hint: Use the syntax 'type ColorKey = keyof typeof colors;' to create a union type of the object's keys.
steps.expectedOutcome: A union type 'ColorKey' is created that represents the literal types 'primary' | 'secondary'.
successCriteria: The union type 'ColorKey' is defined using 'keyof typeof colors' syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a union type that extracts the keys from the const-asserted object.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using 'keyof typeof colors' to create the union type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The union type wasn't created correctly. Remember to use 'keyof typeof colors' syntax.

steps.title: Use the union type in function parameters
steps.instruction: Update the getColorHex function parameter type to use the ColorKey union type you created earlier.
steps.hint: Replace the current parameter type annotation with the ColorKey union type to restrict the function to only accept valid color keys.
steps.expectedOutcome: The getColorHex function will now have a parameter typed with the ColorKey union type, ensuring only valid color keys can be passed.
successCriteria: The getColorHex function parameter type is updated to use the ColorKey union type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully updated the function parameter to use the union type, which provides better type safety by restricting input to valid color keys.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the ColorKey union type specifically for the function parameter type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function parameter type wasn't updated correctly. Check that you're using the ColorKey union type you created earlier.

steps.title: Create a complete example with multiple const-asserted objects
steps.instruction: Create a new function named 'getThemeColor' that accepts a ColorKey parameter and returns the corresponding color value from the colors object.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes a ColorKey type parameter and uses it to access the colors object.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that demonstrates type-safe access to const-asserted object values using the union type.
successCriteria: The getThemeColor function is defined, accepts a ColorKey parameter, and returns the corresponding color value from the colors object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a type-safe function that uses the const-asserted object and union type together.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but check that it accepts a ColorKey parameter and returns the correct value from the colors object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't properly use the const-asserted object and union type. Review how to access object properties with union type parameters.
